analysis.investment_thesis: Blue Jet Healthcare is an operationally superb business — 57% ROCE, near-zero debt, 52% gross margins — but it listed in 2023 at an IPO premium and today trades at 52x earnings and 5.8x book, roughly 2.6x my Graham Number of ~₹161. The catastrophic collapse in operating cash flow from ₹241 Cr in FY2024 to ₹46 Cr in FY2025 is an urgent red flag that requires explanation before any capital commitment.
key_strengths: Exceptional capital efficiency: ROE 52.1%, ROCE 57.3% — among the best I have seen, indicating genuine competitive advantage in contrast media intermediates
Near-debt-free balance sheet (Debt/Equity 0.02) with finance costs effectively zero — the cleanest balance sheet in this cohort by far
Gross margin of 53% suggests proprietary chemistry and pricing power in a niche where few competitors exist
key_risks: P/E of 52x is more than triple my maximum threshold; the market prices in sustained premium returns that may not persist
Operating cash flow collapsed 81% from ₹241 Cr to ₹46 Cr in FY2025 despite net profit of ₹305 Cr — a massive working capital deterioration or accounting divergence that I find deeply suspicious
Revenue has been essentially flat from FY2023 to FY2024 (₹721 Cr → ₹710 Cr), making FY2025's ₹1,026 Cr jump look lumpy rather than structural
red_flags: Recent IPO (listed 2023) — by definition lacks the multi-year public earnings track record I require; the selling shareholders set the price to maximise their own proceeds
OCF of only ₹46 Cr vs net profit of ₹305 Cr in FY2025 implies a cash conversion ratio of just 15% — earnings quality is highly questionable in the most recent year
Free cash flow turned negative (–₹34 Cr) in FY2025 for the first time, coinciding with heavy capex of ₹80 Cr — returns on new capital are unproven
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Graham Number: EPS ~₹17.6 and BVPS ~₹65.4 gives approximately ₹161. At ₹423, the stock trades at 2.6x this ceiling. While this is the most moderate overvaluation among the five stocks, I give it no special credit because it is a recent IPO — the investment bankers and promoters (who retain 79.8%) set the price, not Mr. Market offering a bargain. I distrust IPO pricing by definition: the seller always knows more than the buyer.

The single most alarming data point is the FY2025 cash flow statement: net profit of ₹305 Cr yet operating cash flow of only ₹46 Cr. This implies either massive receivables build-up, inventory accumulation, or other working capital absorption that consumed nearly ₹260 Cr of ostensible earnings. Until management provides a clear reconciliation — and until this normalises — I cannot accept reported earnings at face value. A business with a 15% cash conversion ratio in a given year is not earning what the income statement suggests.
